title: Two eggs, 100 floors: find the breaking floor in 14 drops
description:
You have two eggs and a 100-floor building, and you need the highest floor an egg survives. Dropping every 10 floors can take 19 drops (floor 100, then 91 to 99 one by one). Shrink the jumps instead: drop from 14, then 27, 39, 50, 60, 69, 77, 84, 90, 95, 99, 100, so every extra drop of the first egg leaves one floor less for the second to climb. Whatever floor it breaks on, you're done in 14 drops, because 14 + 13 + ... + 1 = 105 covers 100 floors and 13 drops only reach 91.

Numbers checked in code (every breaking floor tried for both plans, dynamic programming to prove 14 is the minimum, and 100,000 random breaking floors simulated). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming#Egg_dropping_puzzle

beats.say: Not by halving. Drop from floor 50, it breaks, and your last egg climbs from floor 1. That's 50 drops.
Two eggs, 100 floors. Find the highest floor an egg survives. A broken egg is gone, so your last egg goes one floor at a time.
Jump by 10 floors. Worst case, it breaks at 100. That's 10 drops, plus floors 91 to 99. 19.
The flaw: every jump costs a drop, but the climb after never gets shorter.
So shrink the jumps. Start at 14. Then 13 more, to 27. Then 39, then 50.
Breaks at 14? Climb 13 floors. 14 drops. Breaks at 27? 2 drops, plus 12. Still 14.
Why 14? 14 plus 13, all the way down to 1, is 105. Enough for 100 floors. 13 only reaches 91.
So how many drops for 200 floors?
